title: Construction noise near homes: enforcement, penalties and whether thresholds will change
asked: Dr Charlene Chen asked how compliance with construction noise thresholds near homes is enforced and how often it is monitored, how prolonged duration and cumulative exposure are factored into enforcement, and whether the thresholds will be reviewed using psycho-acoustic factors such as sharpness and roughness of sound.
response: Construction sites within 150 metres of homes must install noise meters that NEA monitors, and NEA takes stricter action for repeated offences and for longer periods above the permissible level. Contractors who breach the regulations can be fined up to $40,000 on conviction, plus up to $1,000 a day for continuing offences, with composition sums also possible. NEA will keep reviewing the regulations and permissible noise levels, and psycho-acoustic factors are not currently in WHO guidelines but are part of the science under review. On averaging, the framework uses five-minute and 12-hour averages, and the Minister said Lmax is something the ministry can study.

key_points.point: Construction sites within 150 metres of residential premises must install noise meters, which NEA monitors.
key_points.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
key_points.quote: construction sites within 150 metres of residential premises are required to install noise meters which the National Environment Agency (NEA) monitors

key_points.point: Enforcement is typically more severe for repeated offences and for longer periods above the permissible noise level.
key_points.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
key_points.quote: more severe enforcement action typically taken for repeated offences as well as those with a longer duration of time above the permissible noise level

key_points.point: NEA will continue to review the regulations, including the permissible noise levels.
key_points.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
key_points.quote: NEA will continue to review the regulations including the permissible noise levels

key_points.point: WHO guidelines, which the framework references, currently do not include psycho-acoustic factors, but this is under review.
key_points.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
key_points.quote: which currently do not include psycho-acoustic factors, but this is a part of the science that is under review

key_points.point: Monitoring requirements place a burden on the site operator, potentially including CCTV and continuous real-time monitoring.
key_points.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
key_points.quote: potentially requiring closed circuit television (CCTV), continuous real time monitoring

key_points.point: Failing to comply with the regulations is an offence, with a fine on conviction of up to $40,000.
key_points.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
key_points.quote: shall be liable on conviction to a fine not exceeding $40,000

key_points.point: Continuing offences carry further fines of up to $1,000 a day, and composition sums may also apply.
key_points.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
key_points.quote: further fines not exceeding $1,000 a day

key_points.point: The framework uses a five-minute average sound level as well as a 12-hour average.
key_points.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
key_points.quote: we do have an averaging of five minutes, but we also have some of the framework where it is averaging over 12 hours

key_points.point: Using Lmax, the absolute sound exposure level rather than an average over time, is something the ministry can study, alongside WHO guidelines and international study.
key_points.speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
key_points.quote: It is indeed something that we can study and we will study
